verses.note: Scripture opens without an argument for God's existence. It introduces him by what he does, which is how the whole Bible will go on to make him known.

God reveals himself by a name that stresses his power at the moment Abram's body and Sarai's are past hope. The command comes from the same God who will do the impossible, so obedience rests on who he is.

Abraham names God by what the chapter has shown: a God who kept a promise across twenty-five years and will keep it for generations yet unborn. The title fits a man who owns one well and expects an everlasting inheritance.

God does not answer Moses' sense of inadequacy by building up his confidence but by promising his own presence. The pattern returns in the calls of Gideon (Judges 6:15-16) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6-8), and Jesus' last words in Matthew promise the same presence (Matthew 28:20).
Pharaoh's refusal to know the LORD is the question the plagues answer. God makes himself known not by argument but by acts in history, and the goal is that both Israel and Egypt will know who he is.

God makes himself known progressively. The patriarchs knew him as the God who promised; Israel will know him as the God who keeps the promise. The verse teaches that knowing God's name means knowing his character through what he does.
The command presupposes that the God who spoke in verse 2 is unique in claim and in fact. Deuteronomy 6:4 and Isaiah 45:5 later state openly what this command implies: there is no other.
The verse defines Israel's God by name (YHWH) and by relationship (‘our God’) before any attribute. Whatever the exact grouping of the words, it excludes every rival and claims Israel wholly for him.
David's praise does not stop at the gift but moves to the giver. The confession of God's uniqueness is grounded in what he has done, not in speculation.
God is confessed not only as the source of good things but as the good itself. The psalm's later joys (verses 5-11) all follow from this identification.
